deep.reconstruction:
Context (previous page): Hilbert proposes studying, apart from the invariant theory of binary forms, the polynomials in n variables left unchanged by a single integral linear substitution, and the full system of such invariants. He asserts that polynomials invariant under infinitely many integral substitutions are 'essentially' only the semi-invariants (seminvariants), whose number (of basic ones) is therefore finite.

This page gives a proof sketch.
(i) Let f in C[x_1..x_n] and let G = {g in GL_n(Z) : f(gx) = f(x)}. Suppose G is infinite.
(ii) Claim: G contains an element of infinite order. Hilbert says this follows from 'Minkowski's theorem'. My reconstruction: Minkowski (1887) showed that a finite-order g in GL_n(Z) with g ≡ I mod m, m ≥ 3, equals I. So the kernel of reduction GL_n(Z) -> GL_n(Z/3) is torsion-free. If every element of G had finite order, G would embed in the finite group GL_n(F_3), contradicting that G is infinite.
(iii) Take such a g of infinite order and bring it to canonical (Jordan) form. My reconstruction of the intended case: g is unipotent, or after passing to a power its unipotent part u = exp(N) is nontrivial. Invariance under g then gives invariance under the Zariski closure of <g>, which contains the one-parameter group exp(tN). A Jordan block of size k+1 transforms like the coefficients (a_0..a_k) of a binary form of degree k under x -> x + t y. So f is annihilated by the corresponding Cayley/Aronhold operator Ω = Σ i a_{i-1} ∂/∂a_i, summed over the blocks. Hence f is an ordinary seminvariant (one block) or a simultaneous seminvariant (several blocks). Finiteness then follows from the finiteness of (joint) covariants of binary forms via the Roberts correspondence between seminvariants and covariant leading coefficients.

Second part: a list of properties of the (full) invariant systems, continued on the next page.
1) Invariants are invariant under certain linear transformations of the coefficients, and conversely.
2) They satisfy linear (partial) differential equations, i.e. Cayley's Ω-type annihilators, and conversely.
The next page continues: ring property, algebraic closedness ('volles Formensystem'), the factor property, and the finite basis. This is the programme of Hilbert's 'Über die vollen Invariantensysteme' (Math. Ann. 42, 1893).
errors: The conclusion 'the function is an ordinary or simultaneous semi-invariant' holds only when g (or a power) has a nontrivial unipotent part. If g is semisimple of infinite order, e.g. the hyperbolic matrix [[2,1],[1,1]], the Zariski closure of <g> is a torus. The invariants are then torus invariants, e.g. the norm form x^2 - x*y - y^2, which are not seminvariants in the classical sense. Mixed cases combine both. Hilbert's hedge 'im Wesentlichen' on the previous page only partly covers this.
The step from invariance under the single discrete element g to invariance under the continuous group exp(tN) (Zariski closure) is not stated; it is needed and is true.

'deren Zahl also eine endliche ist' must mean finitely many basic seminvariants (finite generation), not finitely many seminvariants. The finiteness is presupposed from Gordan's theory and not proved here.

results.what: An infinite subgroup of GL_n(Z) contains an element of infinite order, deduced from Minkowski's theorem on finite integral groups.
results.modern_name: Minkowski's lemma: the kernel of GL_n(Z)->GL_n(Z/3) is torsion-free; finite subgroups of GL_n(Z) have bounded order
results.usually_credited_to: H. Minkowski (1887); the general torsion-group statement is Burnside/Schur (1905-1911)

results.what: Polynomial invariants of a single integral unipotent-type substitution reduce, via Jordan form, to (simultaneous) seminvariants of binary forms, hence form a finitely generated ring.
results.modern_name: Weitzenböck's theorem (finite generation of invariants of a linear G_a-action), with the standard reduction to joint covariants of SL_2 (Roberts' isomorphism)
results.usually_credited_to: R. Weitzenböck (1932); proof via SL_2-covariants by Seshadri (1962) and others

results.what: Invariants are characterized by invariance under linear transformations of the coefficients, and equivalently by linear differential equations.
results.modern_name: Cayley-Aronhold differential operators (Ω, O) characterizing invariants and seminvariants

results.what: Programme of 'full form systems' (properties 1-6, continued on the next page).
results.modern_name: Volle Invariantensysteme / algebraically closed subalgebras of the polynomial ring

deep.surprise_reason: The notable item is the sketch. Polynomials invariant under an infinite integral group force an infinite-order element (correctly via Minkowski's 1887 torsion result). Jordan form then reduces the problem to simultaneous seminvariants of binary forms. That is essentially the standard reduction behind Weitzenböck's 1932 finiteness theorem, here in a late-1880s notebook. However, it is a sketch, it overlooks the semisimple (torus) case, and the finiteness itself rests on known Gordan-type results. So it is a notable unpublished anticipation rather than a major result.

checkable.asserts: The integral unipotent substitution (a binary quadratic under x->x+y) of infinite order fixes the seminvariant a1^2 - a0*a2.
The seminvariant is annihilated by the Cayley operator Ω = a0 ∂/∂a1 + 2 a1 ∂/∂a2 (property 2: linear differential equations).

checkable.asserts: The semisimple infinite-order matrix [[2,1],[1,1]] in GL_2(Z) fixes x^2-xy-y^2, a torus invariant rather than a classical seminvariant; this is the gap in Hilbert's claim.

checkable.asserts: The basic unipotent integral substitution has infinite order.
An element congruent to I mod 3 need not be I, but such elements are of infinite order (Minkowski); this is the illustration used in step (ii).
